common_name: Diana's Delight Clematis (Compact Violet-Blue Patio Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; part of Raymond Evison's Boulevard Collection, bred specifically for large pots and small trellises.

directions: Diana's Delight bears rounded, rich violet-blue single flowers with a contrasting boss of cream and gold stamens, opening in flushes from late spring through summer on a compact plant that rarely outgrows a large patio container. Because it flowers on both the previous year's stems and new growth, prune only lightly in late winter, removing dead or weak stems rather than cutting the whole plant back. Keep the root zone shaded and cool with a layer of mulch or a low companion planting while the vine climbs a small obelisk or trellis in full sun, and water container-grown specimens more often than in-ground plants since pots dry out quickly.

common_name: Kingfisher Clematis (Rich Sky-Blue Compact Patio Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; part of Raymond Evison's Boulevard Collection, bred specifically for container growing on a small support.

directions: Kingfisher produces vivid, rounded flowers in a saturated azure-blue with fine red anthers at the center, a striking color combination on a plant compact enough to thrive in a patio pot for years. It flowers in an early flush on overwintered stems and again on new growth later in the season, so prune only lightly in late winter to tidy the plant rather than cutting it hard back. Site containers where the pot itself stays shaded, such as behind lower plantings, while the flowering stems reach into full sun on a small obelisk or wall trellis, and water regularly through the growing season since compact clematis in pots dry out faster than garden-grown vines.

common_name: Parisienne Clematis (Deep Purple Compact Patio Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; part of Raymond Evison's Boulevard Collection, selected for a compact habit suited to pots and small trellises.

directions: Parisienne carries deep violet-purple flowers with a velvety texture and prominent red anthers, opening on a restrained plant that suits a balcony rail planter or patio pot as readily as a small border trellis. Like other Boulevard Collection cultivars it blooms on old wood in late spring and again on new growth later in summer, so limit pruning to removing dead or crossing stems in late winter rather than a hard cutback. Shade the container or root zone with mulch or a low underplanting while the vine climbs into full sun, and water container specimens generously through summer heat to keep the compact framework from drying out.

common_name: Fleuri Clematis (Pale Mauve-Pink Compact Patio Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; part of Raymond Evison's Boulevard Collection, bred for a compact, floriferous habit in containers.

directions: Fleuri opens soft mauve-pink flowers with a paler picotee edge and a cluster of cream stamens at the center, a gentle pastel color that pairs easily with other container plantings. The compact framework flowers in a heavy early flush followed by a lighter repeat later in the season, so prune only lightly in late winter to remove dead or weak growth rather than cutting the whole plant to the ground. Keep the pot or root zone shaded from direct sun while the flowering stems climb a small obelisk in full light, and water container plantings often, since the modest root volume of a pot dries out much faster than open ground.

common_name: Marjorie Clematis Montana (Semi-Double Cream-and-Pink Spring Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Marjorie is a vigorous Clematis montana selection that flowers on the previous year's growth and should be pruned only right after flowering, if at all.

directions: Raised in Devon, England, Marjorie produces semi-double, creamy blush-pink flowers with a warmer salmon-pink flush toward the center, a softer and more layered look than the simple four-petaled blooms of the wild species. It flowers in a single overwhelming spring flush on old wood, smothering a fence, pergola, or mature tree in bloom for several weeks before settling into attractive, undemanding foliage for the rest of the season. Because it can quickly cover 15 feet or more, give it a large, sturdy support and plenty of room, and prune only immediately after flowering if size needs to be controlled, since later cuts remove the following year's flower buds.

common_name: Constance Clematis Alpina (Deep Pink Semi-Double Nodding Bell Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Constance is a compact, early-spring-blooming alpine clematis suited to smaller supports or a large container.

directions: Constance bears nodding, semi-double, rich reddish-pink bell flowers with narrow, twisted inner petaloids that give each bloom extra depth compared to the single-flowered species, opening very early in spring ahead of most other clematis. Like other alpina types it flowers entirely on the previous year's growth, so it needs no regular pruning beyond light shaping right after flowering to remove dead or damaged stems. Its restrained size and cold hardiness make it a good candidate for a large container or a small trellis near a spring bulb display, where the fluffy silver seed heads that follow extend the display into early summer.

common_name: Ruby Clematis Alpina (Wine-Red Nodding Bell Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Ruby is a compact, early-spring-blooming alpine clematis suited to smaller supports or a large container.

directions: Ruby produces nodding, single, wine-red to deep dusky-pink bell flowers with paler, ruffled inner petals, a richer and darker tone than the pale blues and whites more common among alpine clematis. Flowering very early in spring on the previous year's wood, it needs no regular pruning beyond removing dead or damaged growth and light shaping immediately after the bloom finishes. Its modest, restrained habit compared to large-flowered hybrids and montana types makes it a strong choice for a large patio container or a small trellis in a compact garden, and the twisted, fluffy seed heads that follow keep the plant interesting well past bloom time.

common_name: Maidwell Hall Clematis (Rich Blue Double Macropetala Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Maidwell Hall is a compact, early-spring-blooming macropetala clematis suited to smaller supports or a large container.

directions: One of the longer-established macropetala cultivars raised in England, Maidwell Hall bears fully double, rich violet-blue, lantern-shaped flowers with a mass of narrow inner petaloids, a deeper and more saturated blue than many macropetala seedlings. It blooms in mid-to-late spring entirely on the previous year's growth, so it needs no regular pruning beyond removing dead stems and light shaping right after flowering, and the double blooms are followed by fluffy, silvery seed heads that carry interest into summer. Its compact habit suits a small trellis, obelisk, or large container, where it pairs well with late spring bulbs that bloom on a similar schedule.

common_name: Blue Belle Clematis (Deep Purple-Blue Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Blue Belle is a vigorous viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and should be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: Blue Belle produces nodding, four-tepaled flowers in a deep, velvety purple-blue with a paler central bar and contrasting cream stamens, appearing in profusion from midsummer into fall on growth made earlier that same season. As a viticella-type cultivar it resists the wilt disease that troubles some large-flowered hybrids and takes readily to being cut back hard to a foot or so above ground each late winter, which keeps it tidy and encourages the heaviest bloom. Give it a sturdy fence, obelisk, or a shrub to scramble through, since it can easily cover 8 to 12 feet of support in a single season, and mulch the root zone to keep it cool while the vine grows into full sun.
